item.title: Immanent Critique in Management Learning and Education: Organizational Contradictions, Emancipatory Possibilities, and Institutional Transformation
item.content:encoded:
Torkild Thanem, Stockholm University

Shoaib Ul Haq, University of Greenwich

Sara Zaeemdar, Newcastle University

Iain Munro, Newcastle University

Alice Wickström, Aalto University

Farooq Mughal, University of Bath

This special issue addresses an underexplored concern in Management Learning and Education (MLE): the contradictions between the emancipatory ideals espoused by business schools and the institutional, ideological and economic logics they reproduce. Critics have charged MLE with neoliberal, colonial, racist, and sexist practices, which reproduce the harms and injustices of capitalism. However important such work is, these critiques have largely been mounted from a position external to the institutions they target. Less examined is how transformation may be pursued from inside MLE itself, by holding business schools accountable to the very ideals they profess.

The tension is fundamental. Business schools operate as market-driven enterprises while proclaiming educational missions centred on ethics, sustainability, and social responsibility. They continue to train the architects and lackeys of an economic system breaching planetary boundaries while housing sustainability modules that rarely examine the growth imperative running through the wider curriculum. But even though the gap between ecological pedagogy and the ecological consequences of business-as-usual education has become a defining contradiction of the field, such instability also opens space for reimagining the purpose and practice of management education. Institutions that fail to do so risk obsolescence, with their academic freedom further eroded by political intervention or being outdone by AI tools that beat them at their own game of dubious knowledge creation.

Immanent critique offers a particularly valuable method to work through these contradictions and the transformational possibilities that they harbour. In essence, immanent critique combines internal critique with normative critique. Whereas internal critique involves thorough empirical analysis to identify dissonance between institutional claims and reality, normative critique appeals to standards reconstructed from, or held up against, the institution itself. This dual approach lets scholars identify discrepancies between stated missions and operational realities while judging institutions against broader standards of justice and sustainability. Unlike external critique, which imposes outside standards, or ideology critique, which assumes that participants are deluded by false consciousness, immanent critique examines institutions from the inside.

Two things complicate the exercise of immanent critique in business schools. Firstly, business schools speak polyvocally through voices that often pull in opposing directions (through accreditation regimes, faculty research cultures, student demands, donor expectations, etc.). As a result, immanent critique in MLE is no neutral mirroring of declared values but requires careful reconstruction of institutional normativity. Secondly, immanent critique involves the everyday practices of faculty, students, and staff without being confined to the classroom. Such praxis may be enacted on the margins of business schools, through climate occupations and divestment campaigns, anti-war encampments, decolonial reading groups, sanctuary classrooms, strike action and curricular sabotage. Used this way, immanent critique offers a way of revitalising MLE not by indicting it from outside but by internal engagement for institutional transformation.

Working through the internal and external contradictions of business schools, immanent critique turns tensions into pedagogical resources. When business schools claim to educate ethical leaders while prioritising profit maximisation, students can examine organisational hypocrisy not simply as the moral failure of individuals but as structural contradictions requiring systemic solutions. Historical precedent supports this approach: business schools themselves were born of contradictions between professional training and academic legitimacy; contradictions between theory and practice gave way to innovations such as the case method and interdisciplinary curricula. Although these transformations were neither uncontested nor unequivocally emancipatory, they do point to the capacity of MLE to be reconstituted through, rather than against, its internal tensions. Today's challenges call for a similarly fundamental reimagining of purpose and pedagogy.

Methodologically, immanent critique can be pursued through a plurality of approaches. Ethnography is well suited to surfacing contradictions between what people say and what they do, but historical and archival analysis, textual and discursive reconstruction, participatory action research, philosophical reconstruction of institutional norms, and arts-based inquiry are equally legitimate paths into the same problem. By centring the experiences of those inside MLE, immanent critique builds theory from practice and helps close the theory-practice divide in critical management research. The empirical exposition of institutional contradictions also facilitates critique-in-use, that is, forms of critical practice that enable emancipatory change by collectively creating the conditions in which new thinking and new forms of organising may emerge.

Potential topics

  • Theoretical contributions developing immanent critique for MLE contexts
  • Scholarship examining how management education's contradictions relate to broader transformations in capitalism, knowledge production, and subjectivity formation
  • Efforts to rework immanent critique through decolonial, indigenous, and/or feminist epistemologies to address its Western/male-dominated philosophical origins
  • Efforts to develop conceptual frameworks for understanding emancipatory learning within constrained institutional contexts
  • Analyses of how business school commitments to sustainability, EDI, or social responsibility play out in curricular design, pedagogical practice, and institutional governance
  • Ethnographic investigations of alternative management education programs that attempt to embody different values while operating within conventional accreditation and funding structures
  • Studies of alternative institutional forms of management learning, such as cooperatives, free universities, worker-owned schools, platform-cooperative training programs, indigenous-led and faith-based business education
  • Critical investigations of the effects of the rise of far-right political leaders on progressive initiatives in education, such as EDI initiatives, equal pay and promotions, sustainability and ESG measures, and campus protests
  • Participatory research approaches that engage educators and learners as co-researchers in identifying and addressing educational contradictions
  • Arts-based methods for surfacing and representing the affective dimensions of educational contradictions and their role in reproducing or challenging institutional norms
  • Digital ethnographies examining online management education platforms and their claims versus experiences
  • Studies of the pedagogy of growth taught alongside curricula on planetary boundaries, ecological economics, and post-growth alternatives
  • Analyses of sustainability and ESG modules as moments of managerial absorption rather than ecological reckoning
  • Engagements with climate-justice movements as sources of immanent normative reconstruction inside the business school
